story.title: ICE to Spend $20 Million on Electric Shock Gloves for Officers
story.summary: The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to invest up to $20 million in gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks. These gloves are intended to compel compliance from individuals during encounters with officers.

explore_lenses.label: Why could these gloves change ICE encounters?
explore_lenses.title: A close-contact force option
explore_lenses.summary: The proposed device would add an electric-shock option that officers use by physically contacting a person, raising questions about how it would be placed within ICE’s use-of-force rules and supervision.

claims.text: The G.L.O.V.E. is activated from the glove and delivers a shock through direct contact; unlike a Taser, it is not designed to leave burn or contact marks.

The manufacturer’s manual says any force, including this device, may cause or contribute to death or serious injury, and recommends avoiding use on elderly people, small children, pregnant women, and severely disabled people.
DHS says ICE assesses field-equipment needs to support safe arrests and removals and that technology decisions are reviewed for consistency with applicable law-enforcement policies and standards.

explore_lenses.label: How did ICE get to a possible glove purchase?
explore_lenses.title: A procurement proposal, not a completed rollout
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate development is a DHS procurement notice for a potentially large purchase, while the device itself has already been marketed and used in some U.S. corrections and local-law-enforcement settings.

claims.text: According to the DHS notice reported by AP, ICE planned to spend $10 million to $20 million on conductive distraction and de-escalation devices; AP reported that the scale suggested the agency could equip most or all officers and agents.
Sky News reported that the gloves have previously been used by local law-enforcement departments, including in U.S. prison settings.
The manufacturer presents the device as a supplemental tool in an agency’s force continuum, but its manual says the manufacturer does not set agencies’ use-of-force policies or tactics.

story_report.summary: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to spend up to $20 million on wearable devices that deliver painful electric shocks through direct contact, intended to gain compliance during encounters. A DHS notice described the prospective purchase as $10 million to $20 million for “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices”; AP reported that the scale could allow ICE to equip most or all officers and agents. The reporting described a planned procurement, not a completed deployment.

sections.heading: G.L.O.V.E. Device Operation
sections.body: The G.L.O.V.E. is activated from the glove and delivers a shock when it makes direct contact, according to the manufacturer and Sky News. Unlike a Taser, the device is not designed to leave burn or contact marks. The manufacturer describes it as a supplemental option within an agency’s force continuum, while saying that agencies—not the company—set use-of-force policies and tactics. Sky News reported that local law-enforcement departments, including U.S. prison settings, have previously used the gloves.

sections.heading: Safety Warnings and Misuse Concerns
sections.body: The manufacturer’s manual warns that any use of force, including the device, may cause or contribute to death or serious injury. It recommends avoiding use on elderly people, small children, pregnant women and severely disabled people, and says the gloves should not be used for verbal defiance, punishment, torture or horseplay; it suggests a maximum 15-second activation for a specified Level 2 event. Former acting ICE director John Sandweg and law professor Michael Mannheimer raised concerns that ready access could encourage misuse or bypass lesser-force options. DHS said ICE reviews equipment decisions for consistency with law-enforcement policies and standards.

sections.heading: ICE Procurement Timeline
sections.body: AP reported that the DHS notice contemplated a no-bid solicitation as early as Friday and a contract lasting through March 31, 2027. The notice therefore indicated a possible purchasing path, rather than confirmation that ICE had acquired or issued the devices.

unresolved.text: The supplied reporting does not establish ICE’s eventual training curriculum, approved uses, reporting requirements or oversight rules for the gloves.
It remains unclear whether ICE independently evaluated the device’s safety and effectiveness beyond manufacturer materials before issuing the procurement notice.
As of August 13, 2026, the reporting did not confirm that ICE had issued a solicitation, selected a vendor, awarded a contract or deployed gloves to personnel.

related_stories.title: Millions Experience Total Solar Eclipse Across Europe
related_stories.summary: On Wednesday, millions gathered across Europe to witness a total solar eclipse, the first of its kind in nearly 30 years. The eclipse's path of totality passed through parts of Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain, creating a moment of awe as the moon completely obscured the sun. Many other regions, including the UK and France, experienced a partial eclipse, with over 90% of the sun covered in some areas.
